Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 19 distinct packages/libraries: base, blme, broom, dplyr, flextable, forcats, ggplot2, here, knitr, lavaan, lme4, MASS, MplusAutomation, OpenMx, R2spa, SimDesign, tidyr, tinytable, umx. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

The repository holds Mplus code. State the version of Mplus used in the README, and list any add-ons the code needs (for Stata, the user-written commands installed with ssc install; for MATLAB, the toolboxes), so that readers can run the code with the same software.

Parsable code

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 635 columns across 4 data files.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • _import_stressreactivity.R reads mplusdata.csv.
  • _stressreactivity_descriptive.qmd reads mplusdata.csv.
  • StressReactivity_msem.qmd reads mplusdata.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A package could not be installed.

  • sim1.R needs R2spa.
  • sim2.R needs R2spa.
  • StressReactivity_2spa.qmd needs R2spa.
  • sim3_add.R needs R2spa.
  • sim3_revise.R needs R2spa.

R2spa is not on CRAN, and your code does not say where it comes from. If it comes from GitHub or Bioconductor, install it at the top of the script, or name the command in the README, for example remotes::install_github(“user/R2spa”) or BiocManager::install(“R2spa”), with the version you used.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 13 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis

2 _sim1_results.qmd — numeric
3 sim1.R — numeric
4 _sim2_results_supp.qmd — numeric
5 _sim2_results.qmd — numeric
6 sim2.R — numeric

8 _sim3_results.qmd — numeric
9 sim3_add.R — numeric
10 sim3_revise.R — numeric
11 _import_stressreactivity.R — none
12 _stressreactivity_descriptive.qmd _import_stressreactivity.R dependency
13 StressReactivity_msem.qmd _import_stressreactivity.R dependency

File paths

The data paths in the code to files the repository holds work as deposited, but 2 paths name a file the repository does not hold: m2_msem.rds, mplusdata.csv.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: mplusdata.csv.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 13 scripts: 5 ran without error, 3 errored, 0 timed out, 5 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 2 scripts use an object or function that only another script defines, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: _stressreactivity_descriptive.qmd after _import_stressreactivity.R; StressReactivity_msem.qmd after _import_stressreactivity.R. Such a script should source() the other itself, since it does not run on its own.

a script hit an object '...' not found error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first, and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.

This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so it does not force the traffic light red.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

We did not detect an ethics approval statement, and this paper does not appear to involve live data collection from human or animal participants. Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

PubPeer Comments

We checked 50 references with DOIs. No references with comments in PubPeer were found.

We checked 50 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the RetractionWatch database were found.
